source.title: How Far is Video Generation from World Model: A Physical Law Perspective
source.authors: Bing-Yi Kang; Yang Yue; Rui Lu; Zhijie Lin; Yang Zhao; Kai-Xin Wang; Gao Huang; Jia-Shi Feng

page_placements.theme: Aggregate gains conceal instance, subgroup and distributional differences

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study scales video-generation models and data in a different modality, reporting effects on physical prediction and generalization. It does not reproduce language-model loss scaling or fit power laws to its metrics.
record.gate_note: The study reports scaling and generalization results for video models, but its outcomes are velocity-prediction errors, video-fidelity metrics, and human judgments of physical plausibility—not held-out cross-entropy loss or fitted power-law exponents. Those results are recorded with versions ["none"]. The study also discusses scaling and reports results from attribute-prioritization and compositional-generalization experiments; those do not test the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study scales diffusion video models (DiT-S to DiT-XL, 30K to 3M videos; 6 to 60 templates). Its outcomes are velocity error from parsed trajectories, FVD, SSIM, PSNR, LPIPS and human abnormal rates. It reports no held-out loss against scale, fits no power law and estimates no exponents or compute-optimal splits. V5 concerns the power-law form of loss in other modalities, so these task metrics cannot show it. Its 'scaling law' for combinatorial generalization is a monotone trend over three template counts, not a fitted law. These are related constructs, recorded under fits_no_version. The record's 'tests'/T3 overstates the link.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors find near-perfect ID generalization that improves with scale, and OOD failure that scaling does not fix. Combinatorial generalization improves with template coverage and model size. Models generalize case-based, prioritizing color > size > velocity > shape. They conclude naive scaling is insufficient to discover physical laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains diffusion-based video models and evaluates physical-motion prediction and video fidelity; it does not use language models, held-out text cross-entropy, or power-law fitting.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by generalization setting (ID, OOD, or out-of-template), training-template coverage, and model size. The paper reports that OOD velocity error changes irregularly across data scales, while out-of-template combinatorial results improve with greater template coverage.

fits_no_version.finding: For uniform motion, ID velocity error falls with model and data scale: DiT-S at 30K gives 0.022, DiT-L at 3M gives 0.012 (GT 0.010). OOD error stays roughly 0.33-0.43 and varies irregularly with scale; DiT-XL gives no OOD gain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In video diffusion models, scaling improves in-distribution physical prediction but not out-of-distribution extrapolation.

fits_no_version.finding: For DiT-XL, out-of-template abnormal rate falls from 67% to 18% to 10% as templates go from 6 to 30 to 60. DiT-B at 60 templates has a 24% abnormal rate.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Combinatorial generalization in video models improves with training-combination coverage and model size.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuned SVD has larger uniform-motion velocity errors than DiT-B trained from scratch: ID 0.0505 vs 0.0138, OOD 0.9081 vs 0.3583.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Large-scale video pretraining does not fix OOD physical prediction.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025, as stated in the text)
record.problems: The scaling experiments use synthetic 2D simulations and physical-prediction or video-fidelity metrics rather than held-out cross-entropy. No power-law fits or scaling exponents are reported. The paper notes it could not conduct a comprehensive model-size/data-size sweep for the combinatorial task. Several scale trends are described from figures without numerical values in the text, and the reported results provide no error bars or confidence intervals.
record.rows_left_out: Results from the attribute-prioritization, spatial/temporal-composition, visual-ambiguity, and interpolation/extrapolation experiments were left out because they do not report a result on the listed scaling-law versions. Figure-only scale values for the ID/OOD sweeps were not separately extracted beyond the explicitly stated examples; see Figure 3.

untested.parts: No held-out loss versus parameters, data or compute; only a training-loss-vs-steps curve for one model (Fig. 18).
No fit on small runs used to predict larger runs.
DiT sizes vary depth and width together with parameter count; no fixed-parameter shape comparison.
Video models are scaled, but no loss-based power-law form is fitted or tested.
Task metrics are reported against scale for language-model-free video systems, with no predictability or loss-linked analysis.
No exponents or fitting choices are compared.

missing.what: ID/OOD velocity-error values across the full scale grid for the collision and parabola tasks (figure only).
Effect of numeric and text conditioning on ID/OOD error across 30K-3M data for the collision task.

record.verdict_notes: Kaplan et al. is cited only as motivation. The 'scaling law' language in Section 4.2 and Appendix F refers to monotone improvement over three template counts, not a power law. The paper reports no uncertainty.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model loss scaling in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No power-law fit on small runs is used to predict the loss of larger runs.
No fixed-compute optimization of parameter and token allocation.
No controlled comparison of architecture depth, width, or other details at fixed parameter count.
The study tests video-model scaling effects on physical prediction and generalization, but does not measure held-out pretraining loss, fit a power-law form, or estimate its exponents.
No downstream-task performance is related to pretraining loss or scale.
No comparison of power-law fitting choices, exponents, or compute-optimal allocation estimates.

relation.reason: It discusses scaling and its limitations for physical generalization, but does not test or operationally use any listed scaling-law version.

tranche.reason: The study measures physical prediction errors and video quality as model size and data increase, without testing power-law form, fitted extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or downstream performance following pretraining.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is the June 2025 v2. Diffusion models are trained from scratch with a frozen pretrained VAE; qualitative scaling findings do not establish or refute a power law.
